paragraphs: The spring snow had retreated into the shadows of the Zhongnan Mountains, but the mud on Xiliu Plain had yet to dry.

The First Battalion was to hold its inspection before the third day of the third lunar month. Wheel ruts cut uneven grooves into the road outside the drill field. Mist hung over the morning grass; every hoof brought up clods of cold mud tangled in roots. Chang’an had heard that the new army would be on display. Some people carried trays of hot cakes out to sell, while others climbed an old locust tree by the village to see how the Di and the Yan men would fall upon one another.
The lights at the Secretariat burned through the night before the inspection.

Fu Hong worked through the pay registers. The First Battalion was meant to have thirty thousand men. At its first muster, only 27,864 had actually appeared. Some of the missing names were duplicates in the old rolls; some belonged to men ill in other camps; others had been retained by provincial army officials unwilling to release them. Another 1,309 had since been recovered and verified. The inspection roll now held 29,173. More than eight hundred remained disputed or unaccounted for.

Quan Yi said the figure could be presented to the Heavenly King. At the margin Fu Hong wrote instead: “Recheck every absent man, camp by camp.” He had not yet put down his brush when a military clerk announced that two company captains wished to see him. The matter concerned grain being issued in the names of the dead.
The first was a Di captain from Fu Xian’s old company, followed by a deputy captain of Qiang archers. They stood far apart, as though an invisible camp wall still separated them.
“The compensation grain for Fu Xian’s death went to the wrong family,” the Di captain began.
“Who received it?”
“His clan cousin. The military roll lists two sons, but those are the cousin’s children. His only living close relative is his elderly mother in Beidi.”

A clerk checked the old register. Sure enough: wife deceased, two sons. Fu Hong asked why the mother was absent. After much hesitation the captain said she had married again. Fu Xian had been ashamed to mention her. Everyone in the old company knew, but none had cared to correct the record.
“How long ago was the grain paid out?”
“Half a month. Half has been eaten.”

Fu Hong did not know whom to be angry with first. Claiming a dead man’s allowance under false pretenses was real fraud. So was the fact that two children had survived the winter on that grain. He ordered the false claim recorded and what remained recovered. What had already been eaten was to be charged, after the children’s circumstances were verified, to relief stores. The old mother’s allowance must be issued without further delay.
The clerk warned, “Your Highness, if we make an exception here, how many genuine dependants will we uncover in the old books?”
“However many we find, let us first know who they are,” Fu Hong said. “The error is in our military roll. We cannot leave an old woman hungry while we work out a perfect account.”

The captain thanked him but still did not leave. The Qiang deputy had been listening. He placed a small bone tally, worn smooth from handling, on the desk. A name was carved on it in Qiang script, with three short marks on the reverse.
“Machi,” he said, pointing to the tally. “Died in Hexi three years ago.”
“There is no such man on the army rolls,” the clerk answered.
“That is why I’ve come to have him entered.”

Machi was Manu’s elder brother. He had answered a Qin levy under his tribal leader and died on campaign, but his rations had been issued through the tribe. The court’s register recorded how many horsemen that clan provided, never the names of the men themselves. As the deputy explained, his voice grew hard. “He died fighting for Qin. Afterward the books say he never existed. Your grain went to the chief’s tent, and the chief never gave my brother back to us.”
Fu Hong touched the bone tally. The three notches commemorated Machi’s final three battles. It proved that a family had remembered, but did not necessarily prove that he had served in the army.
“Who else remembers him?”
“Five men of his squad, scattered among three stockades in Hexi. Two have lost their legs and cannot come to Chang’an.”

“Have the local army office examine his comrades, the original call-up order, and what he left behind. If the three accounts agree, enter his name and issue the allowance. If the inquiry cannot be completed by winter, pay the family half once the first evidence is checked; hold the rest for verification.”

The deputy appeared not to understand. He had the interpreter repeat the order. When the meaning reached him, he did not kneel. He clasped his hands and asked, “What if the local office still says it knows nothing of him?”
Fu Hong pressed a vermilion seal from the desk onto the paper. “Bring this document back to me.”

As the captains left, the Di man caught sight of the bone tally and said the dead ought not to be added to military rolls on a whim. The Qiang replied with a bitter laugh that some men could even borrow living sons to draw grain. Their argument went a long way down the corridor before fading. Fu Hong knew they would still have to listen to tomorrow’s drums beneath the same banner.
Before noon the new army formed its ranks.

Fu Jian did not ride in the Heavenly King’s ceremonial carriage. He came through the eastern gate on a dapple-gray horse. Villagers stood on field banks beside the road, women lifting their children onto their shoulders to show them the great Qin banners. Three tall standards hung in the mist over headquarters. Only on approaching could one see the neatly sewn patches at their corners. They had been torn in the camp disturbance days earlier; the repairer’s stitches were so fine that the damage was scarcely visible.

Murong Chui stood beneath the reviewing platform in plain iron armor, the new long sword issued by the Qin army at his side. Around his left wrist he still wore an old silver-decorated horse strap from the Yan forces. At the sight of Fu Jian, he dismounted and saluted, then quickly returned his gaze to the ranks.

Three rolls of the drums, and the infantry advanced. At first the formation held reasonably well. When the wings began to close, the trouble appeared. Han standard-bearers turned promptly; Xianbei cavalrymen were accustomed to following the lead horse; Qiang archers still stepped to the sound of their old horns. The right wing was barely opening into a curve when the left pressed inward. Two captains shouted commands at once through the dust, each drowning the other out.

One of the observing princes gave a soft snort of laughter. A startled horse bolted from the ranks, kicked down a wooden stand, and sent men stumbling. Seeing someone fall ahead of him, the recruit Qifu Wu recoiled and almost broke the archers' line behind him. Manu grabbed his collar and shouted in rapid Qiang. The boy understood too little. Liang Hu kicked his shin in frustration, then pointed to the banner above headquarters.
The Qin banner had not moved back.

Qifu Wu looked at it, then at Zhao An scrambling to his feet nearby. At last he checked his retreat. Someone in the rear rank bent to lift the wooden stand. Liang Hu on one side and Manu on the other shoved the recruit back into position. Their five-man squad lurched forward through the dust, none turning to seek the standards of an old regiment.

Elsewhere, Di and Xianbei riders fought for the same narrow lane. Their curses reached the viewing platform; even Fu Rong could hear the different accents. One cavalryman raised his whip by old habit to strike the man beside him. Then he heard the new command from headquarters. The lash changed direction in midair and landed on his horse’s rump. The central signal flag turned again. At last the riders opened a passage along either side.

The sun passed its height. The final drum sounded. Infantry lowered their shields, bows and crossbows moved to the rear, cavalry spread across the flanks. Gaps remained in the formation, and signals reached the outermost ranks half a beat too late. Murong Chui watched without blinking. He saw one troop of cavalry hesitate and was about to send a messenger, but its captain had already lifted the new signal board and filled the gap.
Only then did he raise his hand.
“Close the exercise.”

The standards of the whole camp dipped in succession. The soldiers turned toward the Qin flag above headquarters, raising a disorderly forest of weapons. Iron plates and bowstrings made different sounds in the wind. Among nearly thirty thousand men, not one shouted Murong Chui’s old princely title in unison. A young Xianbei rider instinctively began to cry “Prince of Wu!” and an old squad leader clapped a hand over his mouth. There were tears in the old man’s eyes, as though he hated himself for doing so.
Murong Chui saw him.

In his youth he had broken so many enemy formations with Yan cavalry, ten thousand horses wheeling like a single river. In those days, he had only to raise his sword from the saddle. His soldiers knew its shape. Now he must wait for three signal flags, two chains of orders, and several checked army registers before this distrustful force would move half a li. He did not know whether his old gift was being taken away or he was being forced to learn another way to command.

When Fu Jian entered the central command tent, he asked first how the exercise had gone. Murong Chui answered, “If a real enemy had appeared, the right wing would have broken first. Headquarters changes formation too slowly. Cavalry cannot argue its way through a passage by means of interpreters.”
“Then why did you allow the exercise to end?”
“Because we could still bring the army back into formation.”

The trace of a smile left Fu Jian’s face. Murong Chui moved two wooden cavalry markers beside a narrow track on the sand table. “With enemy riders here, at least two hundred of ours would have died. Give me more time, Majesty. Give every company signalers who can speak two of our army languages.”
“How much time?”
“I don’t know. But it is not a question of marching a hundred thousand men out tomorrow.”
Fu Jian did not press him. He had intended to ask whether this army could obey another commander as readily as it had Murong Chui. Then he noticed the old Yan horse strap around the general’s wrist.
“Still wearing that?”
Murong Chui glanced down. “My eldest son gave it to me. I have worn it in battle for years. I would rather not replace it.”
“Has anyone in the camp accused you over it today?”
“No.”
“Then keep it.”

Murong Chui looked at him. A moment later, he asked that three deputy commanders be appointed under central command, one each for discipline, provisions, and training, without immediately filling Fu Chong’s former post. Fu Jian asked why he was willing to surrender power from his own hands. “A man may know how to maneuver thousands of soldiers,” Murong Chui said, “and still know nothing of the rice jars in ten thousand households. I do not want empty granaries to halt my orders again.”

Fu Jian agreed. By the time they emerged, an evening wind had risen across the drill field. In the distance several Xianbei soldiers were arguing over whether to keep an old Yan bronze helmet. Murong Chui did not go to them. So long as the helmet survived, he knew, Yan would not easily die in those men’s dreams.
At the other end of the field, the pay station was noisier than the maneuvers.

The clerks called soldiers by squads, checked each register, and issued each ration voucher. By dusk more than a hundred men refused to leave. Some complained that they were ten bolts of cloth short; others said their names appeared in both Hedong and Ye, leaving their women and children unable to draw grain in either place. Liang Hu’s squad came last. Zhao An handed over the allowance papers for Helai Yan, with a copy of Machi’s bone tally beneath them.
The clerk did not even look up. “Wasn’t Helai Yan’s cloth issued?”
“Half of it,” Zhao An replied. “The ward elder in Yonghe is holding the other half. He says he needs another document bearing the widow’s handprint.”

Fu Hong overheard and came to inspect the file. The witnesses had signed; every seal was in place. He wrote in the margin that the capital prefecture must recover the rest the next day and have it counted out before the family. He also ordered the responsible clerk’s name written into the register. “Some ward elder” was no longer an acceptable entry.
Beside them the old commandant Fu Su had waited for a long time. He produced a land deed folded into a precise square.
“Before Lord Fu left, he said the court would take our land sooner or later.”
“And you believed him?” Fu Hong asked.

“We all believed him in the old regiments.” Fu Su raised his eyes. “Now seven of my retired comrades have indeed had their fields seized by the county. The decree Your Highness issued said they would not be taken. Can you get them back?”

Fu Hong examined the deed. It bore two different vermilion marks: one from the old military office, the other a new county stamp reading “pending recovery and verification.” The local officials had neither formally confiscated the land nor allowed it to be cultivated. Once the spring planting season had passed, the fields would be wasteland.

He called for a horse and rode to those seven fields before the crowd had dispersed. At the village entrance, an old woman sat beside a ditch mending winter clothes for a son who did not know when he would come home. On seeing the crown prince and his attendants, her first question was, “Are you here to measure our land away?”
Fu Hong crouched and took a handful of damp earth. “Not today. I have come to find out who forbade you to sow it.”

Villagers gathered around, none bowing first. They pointed to the empty wheat ridges and argued over where water used to run, where the ward elder had moved a boundary stone. Fu Hong listened until night began to fall. The order he wrote to the Secretariat was no grand treatise on military reform, only an urgent line: the county magistrate must appear within three days and verify each holding anew; where spring sowing had been delayed, government granaries must advance seed grain.

He finished and looked down at the mud staining his cuffs. By day he had watched thirty thousand men move under one banner. By night he had learned that allowing seven households to plant their own fields in spring might be harder than making thirty thousand blades rise and fall together.
After the inspection, Yao Chang remained General of the Right Guard.

He had served in the capital garrison before. Under the new regulations, checks of seals and passes at the palace gates had become more elaborate. With his old contingents dissolved, only a handful of guards who spoke Qiang remained beside him. Even the warhorse he had ridden in battle had been replaced by an ordinary mount from the imperial stables. His duty room contained former soldiers of Fu Chong, Han officers demoted for faults in the pay registers, and several Xianbei officers.

Yao Chang did not ask them to discuss the new laws. On his first night he toured the western palace gate and found a guard asleep on cold stone, a split in the leather boot on his foot. He ordered an old pair of boots brought out. The soldier thanked him. Yao Chang pointed to the soles. “Who ordered you to keep watch tonight?”
“The court, General.”
“Then put the boots on the court’s account.”

The guard went away uncertainly. A deputy asked why the general would charge the state for boots he had taken from his own house. Yao Chang closed the duty register. “If his feet freeze, who keeps my gate tomorrow night? The government records who missed a watch, not whose shoes let in the wind. The accounts need correcting too.”

The officers in the duty room found those words harder to bear than a denunciation of the emperor. Later that night, over hot broth, they talked again about Fu Chong’s exile. Murong Chui still commanded thirty thousand troops, they said, while old Fu clansmen had lost their place. Yao Chang listened in a corner without a word. When pressed, he replied, “How many of you were there when Lord Fu helped His Majesty conquer the realm? It is not for me to judge his merits and faults.”
“Then you don’t think he was wronged, General?”

“The sentence was written by the Court of Justice and ordered by the sovereign.” Yao Chang blew across his broth. “Read the case before deciding. Shouting grievances on a man’s behalf, without knowing the facts, may only harm him.”

Not a word could be faulted. After the gathering, two former officers went together to the Court of Justice to request copies of Fu Chong’s judgment. The gate clerk permitted it according to the regulations. By the following day, men in the palace were saying that General Yao had demanded they look at the evidence, not chatter carelessly about old victories. Yao Chang heard the rumor and did not correct it. Alone, he counted the arrows issued to the night watch in the armory.
Five days later, Fu Rong brought the latest records from the two investigations to the palace.

He had no single mastermind ready for public execution. Arms had indeed been hidden in the Ye registers case, and Yueshou was not wholly ignorant of it. Fu Liang had used old routes to contact Di stockades; though they could not prove he had sent armor to Ye, his contacts had left a road open to others. Sun Fu had received gold and had been silenced by a false medical attendant: those facts were established. The payer remained in the shadows. Paper used for the forged Chang’an decree came from the old central-command document shop. Exhumation had only deepened the suspicions surrounding the owner’s drowning, without proving which household had given the orders.

Fu Rong spread a map of relay routes across the desk, its lines as fine and tangled as a spider’s web. Some ended at money houses, some at graves, some led into two or three noble residences. Nowhere could he write a final name with confidence.
“Still no one?” Fu Jian asked.
“No one.”
“Then continue.”

“I will.” Fu Rong pointed to a road at the eastern edge. “But perhaps our first assumption was wrong. One man wants to revive Yan; another only wants to keep his soldiers; a third profits from fires. Each pursues his own purpose. None of them necessarily knows that a letter he sends may return to him covered in blood from another man’s knife.”
Fu Jian studied the map for a long time, then had it rolled up and entrusted to Fu Hong. As Fu Rong was leaving, he asked, “What would Brother Jinglue have made of these cases if he were alive?”
“He’d scold me,” Fu Jian said.
“For what?”
“For failing to understand from the start that recovering tiger tallies is easier than winning men’s allegiance.”
Fu Rong managed a tired smile. “And after the scolding, would he help you investigate?”
“He would.”

The brothers fell silent. Wang Meng was gone, but the justice officers still had to rise before dawn to search the roads, and someone still had to ride out when an old villager lost his fields. Fu Jian looked at the pile of memorials he had yet to approve and for a time did not reach for them.
That day another memorial arrived from the south.

It declared that the Jin throne was weak, the southern gentry divided by struggles for power, and that an assault from the north could settle the lands beyond the Yangtze in a single campaign. The language was resplendent; reading it, one might imagine the millions on either bank already holding cups of wine to welcome the Qin army. Fu Jian finished the document and told an attendant to put it on the western desk. He neither endorsed it nor ordered it burned.
That night he went alone to Wang Meng’s former study.

Nobody had sat there for months. Dust lay on the window lattice; beside the old inkstone a drop of pine resin had hardened into something clear as amber. Wang Meng had disliked ornament. On a wooden shelf he had divided his files into groups, their outer tabs marked: Land, Army, Officials, Rivers, Grain, Jin. The world had grown turbulent, but the six words still faced the doorway in silence.

Fu Jian took down the bundle marked Jin. Its last page was an unfinished memorandum written during Wang Meng’s illness. Above were names of generals and provinces, with annotations such as “delay” and “possible.” At the words “campaign against Jin,” the handwriting stopped abruptly, leaving half a page empty.

He remembered Wang Meng grasping his sleeve on the night he died, asking for ten years without an empire-wide invasion of the south. The promise had become an imperial decree; it could not be turned to waste paper because two elegant memorials arrived in spring. Yet the ten years were far from over, and the thought of Jiangnan remained buried deep within him, waking every few nights.
An old writing brush lay at the edge of the table, its tip dry and split. He dipped it in a water bowl, working the bristles gently until they opened. Then he wrote two words: “Defer discussion.”

He studied them for some time, then added a smaller line beside them: “Keep the promise made in Jianyuan Eleven.” The new ink and the old lay on one page, an echo across the border between life and death.

Fu Hong came looking for him, still holding the land deeds from the seven veterans' households. Quan Yi had urged him to return to the Eastern Palace and rest. Instead he opened the study door a fraction and saw his father sitting before a low desk, looking more exhausted than he ever did on the throne.
“Have those matters in Beidi been settled?” Fu Jian asked.

“The county clerk admitted sealing military fields without authority. The land has been restored. But the planting season was lost. Two households received seed grain too late, and their harvests will be poor this year.”
“Whom did you punish?”

“The deputy magistrate’s pay was reduced, and the ward elder suspended pending review. I wanted harsher sentences. Lord Quan says that if we punish every county until no one dares sign a document, the families will still be waiting next year.”
“Do you believe him?”
“Half of what he says.” Fu Hong lowered his eyes. “I’m afraid those two households will go hungry. I haven’t slept properly for days.”

Fu Jian watched his son and remembered himself twenty years earlier, when one error in a small matter seemed enough to bring the whole realm to demand an answer. Later, as the matters grew more numerous, it had become too easy to underestimate the days one person spent hungry.

He took the household papers from the table and handed them back. “From tomorrow, you are to sign as the official in charge of soldiers' pay, military families, and compensation for the First Battalion’s dead and wounded. Quan Yi may challenge you; I shall question you. But every entry must not wait for me to make the first decision.”
“What if I do it badly?” Fu Hong asked.
“Go and see the people harmed by it.”
“And if they refuse to receive me?”
“Then stand outside the gate for a while. Let them finish cursing you. Come back and put it right.”
Fu Hong smiled faintly, bitterly. Fu Jian folded Wang Meng’s paper and returned it to its place. He did not take it away.

The ice in the palace channels had melted. A little stream flowed beneath the steps, tapping softly against the stone corners. Fu Hong saw the new words “Defer discussion” and asked whether his father truly intended to wait the full ten years.
“Jinglue asked for ten years,” Fu Jian answered. “I gave my word. I ought not to stand before his grave inventing another way to count the days.”
“And after ten years?”
“After ten years I shall ask you first. Then I shall ask the realm.”

Fu Hong was about to speak again when the evening drums sounded outside the city. The first beat came too quickly, the second too slowly; the third finally caught the rhythm. Father and son listened for a while. Neither rebuked the drummer.

On leaving the study, Fu Jian looked back. Wang Meng’s wooden desk stood empty. The candle was almost spent. Light fell between the brush rack and old inkstone but did not reach the still-unopened memorials in the corner. He had once believed that a well-governed age needed one or two men to stand before all others and decide for the mountains and rivers of ten thousand li. Wang Meng was gone. Court officials argued, soldiers hesitated, townspeople beat on government doors and cried out their grievances. And still, inch by inch, things moved forward.

A gust of evening wind stirred the old paper labels hanging beside the door. As Fu Jian closed it, he heard one fall to the floor. He bent to pick it up. In Wang Meng’s handwriting, it bore one word: “Grain.”
He restored the label to the shelf and told the keeper to come dust the room the next day. It was not to be sealed.

Next morning, the First Battalion drilled again beyond Chang’an’s eastern gate. Mud splashed across the freshly repaired Qin banner; the horns sounded too quickly, then too slowly. Men who had nearly drawn swords against one another now argued over water at the same trench, and afterward swung their spades together.

Late that night, a courier galloped along the road outside camp, flinging icy mud from his horse’s hooves as he raced toward Chang’an. Liang Hu straightened up from the trench and watched the rider disappear into the dark. Then he bent down again and resumed his quarrel with Manu over their chipped iron spade.
